Title: Regenerative cotton farming package using enriched biochar from cotton stalks combined with bokashi and jeevamrit, delivered through a train-the-trainer model to boost yields, soil carbon, and farmer incomes in Cameroon.
Problem Statement: Smallholder cotton farmers face declining yields, soil degradation, and rising climate stress (erratic rainfall, heat, pests). Conventional practices burn cotton stalks, releasing CO₂ and missing a chance to rebuild soils. The project tackles low productivity and vulnerability by restoring soil fertility and water-holding capacity while reducing greenhouse gas emissions through biochar-based practices.
Solution: The innovation rejuvenates soil health by producing biochar from cotton stalks and enriching it with bokashi (microorganism source) and jeevamrit (microbial “food”). The porous biochar structure retains water and nutrients; combined amendments stimulate microbial activity, improve fertility, and can neutralize acidic soils. Delivery uses a cascade model: 60 agricultural advisors train 3,000 lead farmers, who demonstrate and train ~42,000 farmers via farmer field schools. Early outputs include thousands trained, hundreds of trial plots, >200 t of biochar produced, and preliminary yield gains (from ~1.356 t/ha to ~2.956 t/ha on trial plots). Soil carbon increases are being measured; potential sequestration is ~3 t CO₂-eq/ha/yr.

The training cascade makes regenerative practices practical at scale for smallholders, reinforcing food security and resilience to climate shocks in Cameroon and other cotton growing countries in the Global South.

Competition Analysis:
Status Quo. In Cameroon’s cotton sector, post‑harvest residues are typically burned in the field to control pests. The scaling assessment notes that the biochar used in this project comes from cotton stalks that are normally burnt by farmers in the fields; burning releases additional CO₂, whereas converting the stalks to biochar retains the carbon. These stalks therefore represent a biomass resource that is currently wasted and whose combustion deprives soils of organic matter. Research on crop‑residue management shows that burning wet biomass produces large quantities of CO₂ and fine particulate matter. Although the project documents focus on biochar, agronomic studies have highlighted that intensive use of synthetic fertilisers often leads to soil degradation and poor nutrient‑use efficiency, only 30–50 % of applied nutrients are taken up, with the remainder lost to the environment, and that fertiliser expenses are a substantial cost component in crop production.

Alternatives & Competitive Position. Conventional organic amendments such as compost improve fertility but lack the long‑term structural benefits of biochar. The scaling document describe biochar as a porous product that increases water‑storage capacity, enabling soils to absorb more rainfall and neutralise acidity. The project’s regenerative package combines biochar derived from cotton stalks with Bokashi (a source of microorganisms) and Jeevamrit (a nutrient‑rich microbial inoculant); together these three supplements create a balanced and dynamic soil ecosystem. Preliminary field results in Cameroon support this synergy: on trial plots, average seed‑cotton yields rose from 1.356 t ha⁻¹ in 2023 to 2.956 t ha⁻¹ in 2024/25, an approximate 100 % increase. Because biochar’s carbon matrix is stable, it can sequester about 3 t CO₂‑eq per hectare per year, offering a climate benefit absent from compost‑only systems. By turning a waste product into a valuable amendment and combining it with potent microbial inoculants, this innovation provides a circular, climate‑positive alternative to residue burning or compost alone. Adoption challenges such as labour and knowledge are mitigated through a train‑the‑trainer cascade: 60 agricultural advisors train 3 000 lead farmers, who in turn train 42 000 farmers via farmer field schools, keeping per‑farmer costs low and ensuring wide dissemination.
Scaling Strategy:
Scale through institutional integration of the cascade model: equip advisors (SODECOTON, public services) who train lead farmers to run demonstration plots and farmer field schools. Efficiency: leverages existing networks and locally available feedstocks (cotton stalks), minimizing input costs. Sustainability: embed protocols, budgets, and supervision into partner work plans; align with research partners (IRAD, CIRAD/ICAC) for continuous improvement and monitoring. Responsibility: avoid burning residues; co-design training with local institutions; track participation by women; verify soil-carbon and yield changes before wide rollout. Market engagement will explore private sector interest previously expressed (e.g., Olam Agri/SECO, Mitsubishi) once robust results are published.

The innovation demonstrates a clear and substantial relative advantage over the status quo. The project presentation provides direct, quantitative evidence: "Preliminary yield Increase 1,356 t/ha (2023) to 2,956 t/ha (2024/25)", which is described as a "100 % increase in yield". Compatibility:
Delivered via existing SODECOTON/IRAD advisory structures
The innovation is highly compatible as it is deliberately designed to be embedded within the existing national agricultural system. The Scaling Assessment states: "The innovation can be scaled very easily using the current training model" and explicitly lists the key actors as "Extension worker (ideally through private cotton companies...)" and "Local research institution"
Simplicity & Ease of Use:
# ToT materials/protocols standardized
While the production process has multiple steps (biochar, bokashi, jeevamrit), the Scaling Assessment notes that inputs are "only natural resources (cotton stalks, biomass, etc.)... apart from simple tools and utensils (shovels, buckets, foils/ tarpaulins, etc.)". This indicates the innovation avoids complex technology, relying on accessible materials and skills.
Trialability:
# Demo/trial plots established
The innovation is highly trialable, as proven by the widespread establishment of "239 trial plots (2,39 ha)
Observability:
# FFS sessions showcasing results
The benefits are highly observable and are being actively demonstrated to a large audience. The project has already trained "6.968 smallholder farmers ... via farmer field schools". The very structure of the Farmer Field School (FFS) is designed for observability, allowing farmers to see the side-by-side comparison of treated and untreated plots, as directly quoted by the farmer comparing capsule weights.
Affordability & Cost-Effectiveness:
Input feedstock from cotton stalks (on-farm) and basic equipment (shovel, hoe, bucket etc.)
The primary feedstock is a waste product, making it affordable. The innovation uses "cotton stalks that are normally burnt by farmers" . The Scaling Assessment confirms that "only natural resources (cotton stalks, biomass, etc.) are used here, apart from simple tools and utensils" . This eliminates the need for costly purchased inputs.
